overview.name: OwnStack CLI
overview.tagline: Heroku-style ergonomics on infrastructure you own.
overview.description:
OwnStack is a control plane for deploying apps onto stacks you own.
The CLI scaffolds composable apps, drives local development, and talks
to the control-plane API for deploys, logs, SSH, and more.

Two big ideas:
  - Apps are composed from atomic components (rails, nestjs, react, angular, docs, wordpress).
  - Stacks are infrastructure you own (AWS, GCP, OpenStack, bare metal). One control plane drives many stacks.

Configuration:
  - Global:  ~/.ownstack/config   (OWNSTACK_API_URL, OWNSTACK_API_TOKEN)
  - Project: .ownstack-config     (OWNSTACK_APP_ID or APP_NAME, OWNSTACK_APP_TOKEN)
  - Linked: .ownstack-app         (app id; created by `ownstack remote -a`)
overview.install:
macOS / Linux:
  curl -fsSL https://ownstack.org/install.sh | bash

From a local clone:
  cd /path/to/ownstack/cli && ./install.sh

Verify:
  ownstack --help
overview.auth:
Most control-plane and deploy commands need auth.
  ownstack login                       # browser device-code flow
  ownstack login --token YOUR_TOKEN    # direct (from Settings → API token)
Tokens live in ~/.ownstack/config. Override the API URL with OWNSTACK_API_URL.

commands.name: autobuild holds
commands.summary: List pushes that autobuild held instead of building (supply-chain push watch).
commands.body:
Autobuild does not build a GitHub push to an autobuild branch when:
  - it rewrites history (force-push), or deletes or recreates the branch;
  - a commit carries GitHub's "Merge pull request #N" message but GitHub
    did not commit it (a forged PR merge);
  - a commit claims GitHub as committer and GitHub's API says GitHub did
    not make and sign it, or GitHub cannot be asked (held, not trusted);
  - the branch still contains the head of a hold that was dismissed.
It opens a hold instead, emails the account, and builds nothing. Later
pushes to a held branch fold into the same hold and wait too, because a
normal push on top of a poisoned history builds the poison all the
same. While a hold is open, no other path builds that branch either:
`ownstack deploy` gets 409, and cluster rolls wait.

Calls GET /api/autobuild_holds and prints each open hold: why it was
held, the head commit, its committer, who pushed it, and the apps
waiting on it.

flags.desc: Include released and dismissed holds (history), not only open ones.
Emit the raw /api/autobuild_holds response.

examples.desc: Show what is held right now.
Full history for scripts and agents.

commands.name: autobuild release
commands.summary: Build a held push on every app it was holding.
commands.body:
Usage: ownstack autobuild release <ID> <SHA>. SHA is the head you
reviewed (7 or more hex characters, as `ownstack autobuild holds`
prints it). If another push has folded into the hold since, the
control plane refuses with 409 so you never build a commit you did not
see; list the holds again and review the new head.

Calls POST /api/autobuild_holds/<ID>/release with head_sha. The held
push is replayed through the normal autobuild path (same cluster
routing and CI gate) for exactly the apps on the hold, and monorepo
apps build even if the push did not list their paths, since a
rewritten history's commit list is not a diff. Only account users can
release; developers get 403. Release only a push you can account for.

flags.desc: Emit the raw response (the resolved hold plus deployments_triggered).

commands.name: autobuild dismiss
commands.summary: Clear a held push without building anything.
commands.body:
Calls POST /api/autobuild_holds/<ID>/dismiss. Nothing is built. The
dismissed head stays untrusted: later pushes that still contain it
(checked with GitHub's compare API) are held again, so restore the
branch rather than building on top of it. If the push was not yours:
revoke the pusher's access, restore the branch, then dismiss.

flags.desc: Emit the raw response (the resolved hold).

commands.name: autobuild rules
commands.summary: List, add, enable or disable the pre-build diff screen's rules (superuser).
commands.body:
Before a deploy builds anything, the control plane diffs the commit it
is about to build against the app's last deployed commit and matches
every added line, and every changed font/image-looking file, against
these rules. A match holds the deploy (category supply_chain) and opens
an autobuild hold with the rule, file:line and an excerpt; see
`ownstack autobuild holds`. Releasing the hold approves that commit.

Rules are rows on the control plane, so a new pattern applies to the
next deploy with no release. Patterns are Ruby regular expressions with
a 0.5s match timeout (a timeout counts as a match, not as safe).

Usage:
  ownstack autobuild rules [--json]
  ownstack autobuild rules add <KEY> --description=D --line=RE [--path=RE] [--exclude=RE] [--kind=added_line|disguised_asset]
  ownstack autobuild rules enable|disable <KEY>

Kinds: added_line (an added line matches --line), disguised_asset (a
matching path whose content is text), changed_file (any change to a
matching path), package_scripts (a package.json script the build runs
changed, compared as parsed JSON), package_dependency_source (a
dependency now comes from a URL, git or a local path).

Defaults (calibrated on the 2026-10-27 attack and measured on real
history): package_scripts_changed, dependency_from_url,
build_control_file_changed (Dockerfile, Procfile, app.json, npm/yarn/pnpm
config, buildpack hooks, Gemfile, .gitattributes, .vscode/),
code_hidden_after_whitespace, code_disguised_as_asset,
lifecycle_script_runs_local_file, install_hook_added,
editor_autorun_task, editor_auto_tasks_allowed, and
very_long_source_line (off: it flagged long prose in real data files).
A monorepo app is screened on its own subdirectory plus repo-root files.

flags.desc: Emit the raw rules list.
For added_line rules, the pattern an added line must match.
Only files whose path matches (default any).
Skip files whose path matches (generated files, lockfiles).
added_line (default), disguised_asset, changed_file, package_scripts or package_dependency_source.

commands.name: remote
commands.summary: Show or set the control-plane app linked to this repo, or run one remote command against any app.

flags.desc: With nothing after it, link this repo to the app (by name or id). With a command after it (restart, logs, deploy-log), run that command against the app without linking or writing anything.

examples.desc: Show the currently linked app.

commands.notes:
Linking creates `.ownstack-app`, stores your token in `.ownstack-config`, and makes that
token the app's deploy token on the control plane. Outside a git work tree it asks
first, and a non-interactive run refuses unless you pass `--yes`. (The check is "inside
some git work tree", so a subfolder of an unrelated repo still links without asking.)
`remote -a APP <command>` never links: it runs restart, logs or deploy-log against APP
for that one call. Other remote subcommands (stop, start, status, shell, run, open) use
this repo's Dokku git remote and do not take -a.
If the directory is already linked to a *different* app, linking is refused so you
don't clobber another app's link by standing in the wrong repo (a common footgun with
`ownstack app create`, which auto-links the current directory). Pass `--relink` to
override, or `cd` to the intended app's directory first. Re-linking to the same app is
always allowed (it just refreshes the deploy token).

commands.notes:
Usage: `ownstack remote restart [TYPE]`. With TYPE (e.g. worker), only that process type restarts (`dokku ps:restart APP TYPE`). If the control
plane does not confirm a single-type restart (an older server restarts everything), the
command warns and exits 1 rather than claim it restarted only TYPE.
Without TYPE it halts and restarts running processes (web + workers). This is what applies config
vars written with `ownstack config:push --no-restart`, since Dokku config:set runs
with --no-restart and leaves running containers on their old environment.

commands.name: deploy:verify
commands.summary: Check what each stack is actually running against what the control plane recorded as deployed.
commands.body:
Reads, on each stack, the containers dokku serves the app from and the
commit each was built from (its GIT_REV), next to the control plane's
last "deployed" commit for that stack. Verdicts: match, mismatch,
not_running (a recorded container is gone or stopped), no_containers,
no_recorded_deploy, unreadable. Exits 1 unless every stack matches, so
it can gate scripts.

Why: during the 2026-10-27 supply-chain incident deploys reported
"deployed" while the old containers kept running (control-plane#1339).
Deploys now verify this themselves and fail as release_unverified; this
command checks any app on demand, including ones deployed before that.
Calls GET /api/apps/<id>/running_release.

jobs sent from the control plane. Opt-in per stack: when enabled,

commands.name: stack add-ons
commands.summary: List, add, and remove a stack's add-ons (Heartbeat, Private Network).
commands.body:
Stack add-ons are opt-in per stack; nothing is added by default.

Private Network (`tailscale`) joins the stack's host to a tailnet you
own: Tailscale, or your own Headscale server via `--login-server`.
You bring the auth key. OwnStack holds it (encrypted) only until the
background join uses it, then discards it; it never appears in a
command line or log. The join takes about a minute; `add-ons <STACK>`
shows joining, joined (with the tailnet IP), or failed (with why).

What joining changes on the host: tailscaled runs, and peers your
tailnet ACL allows can reach the host's listening ports over the
tailnet (restrict that with tailnet ACLs). What it does not change:
the host's DNS resolver (MagicDNS is not applied), and how OwnStack
reaches the host (still its public address). A host already on a
tailnet OwnStack did not set up is left alone. Owner-only: share
recipients and developers can't add or remove it.

Use `list` explicitly if a stack is named add, remove, or list.

flags.desc: Emit the add-on list as JSON.
Tailscale auth key (tskey-auth-...) or Headscale pre-auth key. Prompted for (hidden) when omitted, which keeps it out of shell history.
https URL of your Headscale server. Omit for Tailscale.

groups.title: Clusters and load balancing
groups.body:
A cluster pools stacks behind a hostname. It owns a Caddy proxy app (deployed to N proxy stacks
for redundancy) and routes traffic to member app-stacks. Pick the edge mode at create time:
  - dns_rr      DNS round-robin. Free, works anywhere.
  - cloudflare  Proxied origins, sub-second failover.
  - aws_alb     AWS ALB (LBaaS).

The proxy app is just an OwnStack app — same logs / restart / SSH / scale / maintenance as
anything else. The cluster regenerates its Caddyfile on member changes and dokku-deploys it.

commands.name: config:push
commands.summary: Push managed config vars to a deployed stack and restart it so they take effect.

flags.desc: App name. `--app NAME` works too. Defaults to the linked app only when the flag is absent: the flag is never ignored, so it can no longer answer with another app's vars.
Target stack (required when the app has more than one stack).
Store the vars without restarting. Running containers keep the previous values until the next restart or deploy.

commands.notes:
Applies the control-plane config vars to the stack via dokku config:set, then
restarts the app so the running containers pick them up. Pass specific KEYs to
push only those; omit to push all.

The restart is the part that matters. Dokku config:set runs with --no-restart so
the write is instant, which means the vars sit in Dokku's store while every
running container keeps its old environment. Verifying with `ownstack run printenv
MY_VAR` does not catch this: `run` starts a fresh one-off container that reads the
new value regardless. Check `ownstack stack containers <STACK> --app=<APP>` instead
and look at the container age, or trust this command to restart for you.

With --no-restart, apply the vars later with `ownstack remote restart` (or
`ownstack app restart <APP>`) or on your next deploy.

commands.summary: Manage scheduled jobs that run via `dokku run <app> <command>` on the stack's crontab.
commands.notes:
The control plane keeps a managed block in the dokku user's crontab,
delimited by `# OWNSTACK-CRON: <dokku-app> BEGIN/END` markers. Any
add/update/remove triggers a re-push to every deployable stack. Use
`cron:sync` to force a re-push without changing the job set (useful
after restoring a stack or recovering from drift).

Schedule is standard 5-field cron (`minute hour day-of-month month
day-of-week`). Commands run inside `dokku run`, so use your app's
process binary directly (`rake db:cleanup`, `python manage.py jobs:run`).
`%` in the command must be escaped as `\%` — cron treats unescaped
`%` as a stdin separator.

explicitly if an app is named add, remove, or list.

groups.title: SSL certificates
groups.body:
Certificates live in an account-scoped "locker" (`/api/ssl_certificates`).
Each cert can be pushed to one or more apps; pushing writes the cert into
Dokku's per-app `tls/` directory and rebuilds nginx with a `listen 443 ssl`
block. Pushes are asynchronous — the CLI enqueues a `SslCertificatePushWorker`
job and polls for the result before reporting success/fail per stack.

DNS for Let's Encrypt (DNS-01): domains whose zones live in OwnStack's
platform Hetzner Cloud DNS need nothing connected. The control plane
writes the challenge records to Hetzner itself, for issuance and for
auto-renewal. For a domain hosted in your own AWS account, connect
Route53 (`ownstack route53 connect`). DNSimple is a legacy, optional
integration (`ownstack dnsimple`), kept for zones still hosted there;
it is not required for anything. To issue a cert locally, `sslgen`
defaults to Hetzner Cloud DNS (token from `HCLOUD_TOKEN` or the hcloud
CLI config), with `--dns route53` and `--manual-dns` as alternatives.

commands.name: cert publish
commands.summary: Upload a sslgen cert (fullchain.pem + privkey.pem) to the locker, then push to an app.
commands.notes:
Each invocation uploads a new locker entry. To attach the same cert
to multiple apps without duplicates, run `cert publish` once and then
`cert push --cert-id=N --app=APP` for each additional app.

Issue the cert first with sslgen, which answers the DNS-01 challenge
on Hetzner Cloud DNS by default:
`sslgen request example.com` (writes ~/.sslgen/certs/example.com).
Test with `--staging` first; use `--dns route53 --aws-profile NAME`
for a Route53 zone, or `--manual-dns` for anything else.

commands.notes:

Cloud DNS (automatic, nothing to connect) for domains in OwnStack's
Hetzner zones, otherwise a connected Route53 integration
(`ownstack route53 connect`), or the legacy DNSimple integration if
one is connected. It then updates the locker entry in place and
re-pushes to all apps whose `ssl_certificate_id` references the cert.
Issuance takes a few minutes; the CLI polls until the job completes.
Certs expiring within 30 days renew automatically (when auto-renew is
on, for integrations). This command is for renewing on demand.

groups.title: Pipelines (staging → production)
groups.body:
Heroku-style staging → production flow. Each app gets one pipeline (created on first
deploy or via `add-staging`). Stages are tagged by name — anything matching /staging/i
is the staging stage; /prod(uction)?/i is production. The staging stage is a first-class
app (`<app>-staging`) with its own config vars, database, domains, and autobuild toggle:
leave autobuild on for staging and turn it off on production, and pushes to the tracked
branch deploy staging only. `promote` ships staging's exact image to production
(buildless, `dokku git:from-image`) when both stages share a stack; the production
release phase (migrations) runs against production config as usual.

commands.notes:
App must have a successful production deploy first. The production stage is
auto-created on first deploy; staging reuses the same stack. The staging app gets
its own postgres/redis links and rides the production repo webhook for autobuild.
To stop production from auto-deploying on push, run
`ownstack app autobuild:disable <app>` and keep autobuild on for `<app>-staging`.

commands.name: pipeline promote
commands.summary: Ship staging's release to production (buildless image promote when possible).
commands.notes:
Same-stack stages: the running staging image is pinned
(`dokku/<prod>:promote-<sha>`) and deployed via `dokku git:from-image`, so the
exact tested artifact ships with production config vars and release phase
(migrations). Different stacks or missing image: falls back to rebuilding
staging's last successful commit. Refuses while a staging deploy is in flight.
Output says which strategy ran. Tail with `ownstack remote deploy-log`.

Connection saturation is a common cause of deploy failures on these
stacks: during a deploy the old containers keep running, so the
release one-off has to fit on top of the steady-state worker pools.
If usage sits near max_connections the release task dies with
"FATAL: sorry, too many clients already". This command makes that
visible without dropping to `dokku postgres:connect` + raw SQL.
Warns at >70% of max_connections, flags red at >85%.

groups.title: Postgres backups (object storage)
groups.body:
Per-app Postgres backups to object storage (S3, GCS, or DreamObjects),
mirroring Heroku's `pg:backups`: capture, list, download, restore, and a
scheduled backup with a grandfather-father-son (GFS) retention calendar.

Backups are captured on the stack via `dokku postgres:export`, uploaded to
the object storage configured for the app's stack, and pruned on the
retention calendar. Each backup has a short id (e.g. `b042`) and is
individually downloadable and restorable. The destination credential and
bucket come from the stack's backup configuration unless overridden.

groups.title: AI coding agents
groups.body:
An agent is a long-lived AI coding worker bound to a codebase and running
on a stack you own. It is its own resource, not a flag on an app: one
repository can host several agents, and an agent does not require a
deployed app at all.

Each agent gets its own unix user on the stack (ownstack-agent-<id>, no
password, no sudo) and its own checkout at /var/ownstack/agents/agent-<id>,
mode 0700 and owned by that user, so agents on a shared stack cannot read
each other's source. Claude runs as that user on your Claude subscription,
signed in one of two ways: with one of your Claude tokens (`ownstack agent
claude-token add`, from `claude setup-token`, one per Claude account, set
once for all your agents), or with its own `claude auth login` on the
stack. No Anthropic API key is used, ever.

Requires the `platform.agents` capability, which is off by default for the
developer role and granted by a manager via `ownstack developers update`.

commands.name: agent list
commands.summary: List agents with status, whether each can run (USABLE), Claude sign-in (CLAUDE), stack, repo, and branch.

examples.desc: Same list. `ownstack agents SUBCOMMAND` works like `ownstack agent SUBCOMMAND`.

commands.notes:
STATUS is the workspace's state, so an agent can read `ready` and still be
unable to run. USABLE and CLAUDE come from the API's `usable` and
`authenticated`. Below the table, each agent that cannot run gets one line
saying why (the first sentence of its readiness), for example
`probe-agent: stack is not provisioned.` A `-` means the control plane
does not report that field.

commands.name: agent create
commands.summary: Create an agent. The workspace is cloned on the stack in the background.

flags.desc: Stack to run on (required).

Git repository the agent works on. Required unless --app is given. An https URL clones with your linked GitHub login. An SSH URL (git@host:owner/repo.git or ssh://user@host[:port]/path) clones and pushes over SSH, with a git key (see --git-key), never rewritten to https.

For an SSH URL: a git key from your SSH Locker (kind git) to clone and push with; you put its public key on the repo. Without it, OwnStack makes an ed25519 key for this agent in your SSH Locker and, on github.com, adds it to the repo as a deploy key with write access using your GitHub login. The key leaves the repo and the locker when the agent is destroyed.
Branch to check out (default main).
Bind to an app; repo, branch, and monorepo subdir are inherited when not given.
Monorepo subdirectory the agent works in.
Require confirmations instead of running with --dangerously-skip-permissions.

How the agent signs in to Claude: auto (the default; your Claude token when you have one, otherwise its own sign-in), owner-token (always your Claude token), or own-sign-in (its own claude auth login on the stack).
Pin one of your Claude tokens (by label or id, see agent claude-token). `default` (the default) uses whichever token is your default.

examples.desc: Inherit the repo from an app but work on a different branch.
Over SSH, with a key OwnStack makes and adds to the repo as a deploy key.
Over SSH to another git host, with a key from your SSH Locker.

commands.notes:
Requires jq. An agent name is lowercase alphanumeric and dashes, unique per account.
Over SSH the host key is pinned: github.com's from GitHub's API, any other host's read once
with ssh-keyscan on the first sync and kept with the key, so a host key that changes later
fails the sync instead of being trusted. If the host refuses the key (for example, OwnStack
could not add the deploy key because your GitHub login lacks admin on the repo), the agent
fails with the public key to add; add it and run `ownstack agent sync NAME`.

commands.name: agent show
commands.summary: Full state for one agent, including whether it can actually run.
commands.notes:
`usable` is only true once `claude auth status`, run on the stack as the
agent's unix user, reports a signed-in session. A synced workspace on its own
is not enough: an agent that is not signed in reports `usable: false` and
explains why in `readiness`, rather than failing on the first prompt.

`claude:` is what Claude is doing on the stack right now (working, waiting
for you, idle, or no open session), followed by one line per recent Claude
session, from a terminal or a run. It comes from the Claude Code hooks
OwnStack installs for the agent's user on each sync; they report only the
hook event and session id, never prompts or tool output. A working session
that has been silent for 15 minutes is marked "no activity for a while" and
no longer counts toward `claude:` (Claude may still be thinking, or the
process may have died or been interrupted). A run's session ends when the
run does.

`live status:` says whether the stack proved it can report (a round trip
made from the stack at sync), or why not. Against a control-plane without
this feature, `claude:` says it is not reported rather than guessing.

`claude sign-in:` says how the agent signs in to Claude right now, in the
control plane's words (for example "Uses the Claude token of
me@example.com."), followed by the stored setting (auto, owner-token, or
own-sign-in). An agent that uses its owner's Claude token can only be run,
and its terminal opened, by that owner.

`claude token:` is the token the agent would use (label and last 4 only),
marked `(pinned)` when set with --claude-token, otherwise `(default)`.
`active token:` is the token installed on the stack right now, which
differs after an automatic switch. `last switch:` is the reason and time
of the last automatic switch, for example when a token hit its Claude
usage limit and the agent moved to the owner's next usable token.

To get one, run claude setup-token on your own computer, approve in the browser, and paste the token it prints (it starts with sk-ant-oat01-). It is stored encrypted, only your agents use it, and it is good for a year. It uses your Claude subscription; it is not an Anthropic API key.

commands.notes:
How to get one: on your own computer (where you use Claude Code), run
`claude setup-token` and approve in the browser. It prints a token that
starts with sk-ant-oat01-. It uses your Claude subscription and is good for
a year. It is not an Anthropic API key, and none is needed. Add one per
Claude account, labeled so you will recognize it (for example the
account's email).

add and rotate read the token from stdin, or prompt with hidden input at a
terminal. A token is never taken as an argument or flag, so it stays out of
shell history and process lists; the CLI refuses one without echoing it.

Tokens are yours alone: each OwnStack user adds their own, and an agent
uses only tokens of the user who created it, never another member's. They
are stored encrypted and no command or endpoint shows one again (only the
label and last 4 characters). An agent uses your default token unless it is
pinned to one with `ownstack agent update NAME --claude-token=LABEL`.

When the token an agent is using hits its Claude usage limit, OwnStack marks
it limited until its reset time, switches the agent to your next usable
token, and continues the run. Once the limit resets, the agent switches back.
`list` shows the limited tokens and why.

Labels match case-insensitively; a label wins over an id. A rejected token
or label prints the control plane's reason as is.

commands.name: agent login
commands.summary: Sign an agent in with your Claude subscription (no API key, ever), then confirm it worked.

flags.desc: Re-check the sign-in on the stack and wait for the answer. This is a sync, the same thing the page's "Done, re-check agent" button does, so it re-fetches the branch (reset to origin) and the agent cannot run until it finishes. If a sync is already running it waits for that one first. Exits 0 when signed in, 1 when not.

commands.notes:
The sign-in itself happens on the agent's page in the web app. Choose
"Sign in to Claude" there: it opens a terminal on the stack as the agent's
unix user and runs `claude auth login`. Finish the claude.ai sign-in in that
terminal (open the URL it prints, approve, paste the code back). The
sign-in persists in the agent user's home on your stack. This is the
own-sign-in path; to skip it for all your agents, add your Claude token
once with `ownstack agent claude-token add --label=LABEL`.

At a terminal, `login` opens that page, waits for Enter, then checks. In a
script or pipe it prints the page and the next step,
`ownstack agent login NAME --check`. An agent that is already signed in
says so and exits 0.

The web app URL is derived from the API URL (api.<domain> becomes
my.<domain>). Set OWNSTACK_WEB_URL to override it.

commands.summary: Re-create the workspace on the stack and fetch the branch.

commands.name: agent exec
commands.summary: Run a command inside the agent's workspace on its stack.

flags.desc: Subdirectory of the workspace to run in. Relative to the workspace only.
Give up after SECONDS. Default 120, capped at 900.
Set an environment variable for the command. Repeatable.

examples.cmd: ownstack agent exec backend-dev -- bundle exec rspec
ownstack agent exec backend-dev --cwd=frontend --timeout=600 -- npm run build
ownstack agent exec backend-dev --env=RAILS_ENV=test -- bin/rails db:migrate
ownstack agent exec backend-dev -- grep -E "TODO|FIXME" app/models/user.rb
examples.desc: Several arguments arrive exactly as typed; the | stays inside the pattern.

examples.cmd: ownstack agent exec backend-dev -- "cd frontend && npm test | tail -20"
examples.desc: One quoted argument runs as a shell command, pipes and && included.

commands.notes:
Everything after `--` is the command, passed through untouched, so a command
containing its own dashes works. With several arguments, each one reaches the
stack as you typed it: quotes, `$VARS`, `|`, globs, and spaces inside an
argument stay part of that argument, much like `docker exec`. The command still
runs under bash, so a leading `VAR=value` word sets an environment variable and
a first word like `time` acts as the shell keyword. With a single argument, it
is run as a shell command string, so a pipeline or `&&` goes in one quoted
argument. Because of that, never pass untrusted text as the only argument
(`-- "$file"` runs it as shell code; `-- cat "$file"` is safe). The exit code
you get back is the command's
own, which means this composes in a script the way `ssh` does; a transport
failure uses 125 so it stays distinguishable from a command that genuinely
failed.

Output is capped at 512KB per stream on the stack side. When that cap is hit
the command says so instead of quietly handing you a truncated log.

What this is and is not: the command runs as the agent's own unix user with
that user's rights. Paths are confined to the workspace, so you cannot point `--cwd`
outside it, but a command is free to walk out on its own. The real boundary is
who is allowed to hold an agent at all (`platform.agents`), not the path check.

groups.title: Operator agents
groups.body:
Reach the agents in your operator channel (the Slack operator), on this
computer or on a stack. `ownstack op` is short for `ownstack operator`.

An agent on this computer is a seat the operator CLI (~/bin/operator)
saved in ~/.ownstack-operator, with its agent running in its own tmux
(`tmux -L ownstack-operator`, never your own tmux). These commands find
the seat and hand off to the operator CLI, so attach and the agent server
have one implementation.

A stack agent is one from `ownstack agent list`. Its agent server, when it
has one, runs on the stack as the agent's unix user. Attaching opens an
interactive SSH to the stack (the same credentials `ownstack ssh stack`
uses) and attaches to that user's tmux session. When a name is both a seat
here and a stack agent, the seat here wins.

Seat tokens never pass through this CLI. A stack agent gets its seat and
agent server when it is invited from Slack
(`/ownstack operator invite HANDLE --agent AGENT`).

One stack agent can hold several seats. Each is a named session: its own
Claude conversation and tmux session, named by its seat's handle, on the
same box and unix user with the agent's one set of logins (the agent is
the security boundary; a session is a conversation inside it).
`operator sessions AGENT` lists them; `operator attach AGENT SESSION`
opens one. The agent server keeps each one running, and when OwnStack
switches the agent's Claude token (a usage limit, or a reset) it restarts
each session resuming its own conversation.

commands.summary: Jump into an agent's tmux session (for a stack agent, one of its named sessions with SESSION). With no agent, list the agents you can attach to, here and on your stacks.

flags.desc: Watch only. Nothing you type reaches the agent. Detach with Ctrl-b d.
Open it as a native iTerm2 window (operator serve attach --iterm). Agents on this computer only; refused with a clear message when the installed operator CLI does not support it yet.

Print the command it would run (operator serve attach, or the ssh and tmux target), and run nothing.

commands.notes:
From GET /api/agents/:id/sessions. State is working, waiting (needs you),
idle, ended, or limited (Claude said its account is out of usage); a `?`
means nothing was heard from it for a while. Anyone who can see the
agent sees names and state. Its owner, who may open its terminal, also
sees each session's tmux session, working directory, transcript path and
`ownstack op attach AGENT SESSION`.

commands.name: operator server
commands.summary: Put an agent on an agent server so it stays reachable after its session ends.
commands.notes:
On this computer it runs `operator --as AGENT serve adopt`, which finds the
seat's working directory and Claude conversation and puts it on this
computer's agent server (installing the server if needed). When the
installed operator CLI has no `serve adopt`, it fetches the current one
from https://bot.ownstack.org/operator/cli, checks it parses and has
adopt, and only then replaces ~/bin/operator. A seat already served
shows its status instead.

For a stack agent it runs one command on the box through the exec API:
a box holding exactly one seat gets `operator serve install` for it, in
the agent's work dir; a box already served shows `operator serve

groups.title: Operator in Slack
groups.body:
Operator puts agents in a Slack channel as members: you @ one to hand it
something, DM it, or talk to all of them, and they post back under their
own handle. It is driven from Slack with the OwnStack bot's slash command,
`/ownstack operator` (`/ownstack op` is short for it), not from this CLI.
`/ownstack op` with no verb lists every verb.

Common verbs, typed in the Slack channel:
  - `/ownstack op invite <handle>`: invite an agent. You get a line to paste
    to it, once. The first invite in a channel turns Operator on there.
  - `/ownstack op invite <handle> --agent <stack-agent>`: seat an OwnStack
    stack agent (one from `ownstack agent list`). It installs an agent server
    on the agent's box that keeps it running and answering in the channel.
  - `/ownstack op invite <handle> --remote --repo <git url>`: an agent on an
    OwnStack server, created with your OwnStack login.
  - `/ownstack op who` and `/ownstack op status`: seats, last seen, and what
    each agent is working on, blocked on, or asking you.
  - `/ownstack op agent server [install | update | restart | stop | start | peek] [handle]`:
    the agent servers in the channel.
  - `/ownstack op off` / `on`, `revoke`, `rename`, `quiet`, `unquiet`, `members`.

How it relates to the CLI: an invited agent talks to the channel through the
operator CLI (`~/bin/operator`, from https://bot.ownstack.org/operator/cli).
`ownstack operator` (`ownstack op`) works with those agents from your
computer: attach to an agent's session, put one on an agent server, or see
the agent server's status. Instructions for agents joining a channel:
https://bot.ownstack.org/operator

groups.title: The World (every session at a glance)
groups.body:
The World shows every session you have in one place: the named sessions on
your stack agents and the Operator seats on your own computers. In the 3D
World each stack agent or computer is a tower and each session is a floor,
colored by what it is doing.

All three views read one feed, `GET /api/world` on the control plane, with
your OwnStack token (pass `OWNSTACK_PROFILE=NAME` inline to pick an
account). The control plane adds Operator data from ownbot; when ownbot
cannot be reached the feed still has your stack sessions and says Operator
data is unavailable.

A session's state is one of: working, waiting (needs you: an open question
or a blocked status), idle, limited (out of Claude usage until the time
shown), stopped, ended, or offline (its stack agent or computer cannot be
reached).

commands.notes:
WHERE is the stack agent or computer the session lives on. SLACK is its
Operator seat's channel, or `-` when it has no seat. TOKEN is the Claude
token its stack agent uses (label and last 4), or `-`. States are colored
on a terminal (working green, waiting yellow, idle dim, limited magenta,
stopped, ended and offline grey); set NO_COLOR to turn colors off.

The page loads the 3D scene from
https://my.ownstack.org/assets/world/world.js and puts your feed inline
as `window.WORLD_DATA`, escaped so no field can break out of the script
tag. If the scene cannot be loaded it says the scene is not published
yet and lists your sessions instead of showing a blank page. With
`--watch`, a scene that defines `window.WORLD_UPDATE(data)` is updated
in place; otherwise the page reloads when the data changes.
`OWNSTACK_WORLD_ASSET_BASE` points the page at another copy of the scene
(for working on the scene locally). The scene's "create a stack agent"
link points at /agents on the same host as the scene.

commands.name: world --tui
commands.summary: The World live in this terminal. A tower per stack agent or computer, a floor per session, a Waiting on you box and an activity ticker.
commands.notes:
Refreshes every 5 seconds. Keys: arrows or j/k move between sessions,
Enter attaches to the selected session (runs its attach command, such as
`ownstack op attach my-agent dns-claude`, and comes back to the World
when you detach with Ctrl-b d), c copies the attach command (or prints
it when there is no clipboard), r refreshes now, q quits. Waiting floors
carry a `!`. The sky follows your local clock, the elevators run, and a
session that finishes (working to idle) gets a small celebration.

It only runs attach commands that are plain `ownstack ...` words. On a
narrow terminal it shows a list instead of towers; NO_COLOR works, and
each floor also shows its state in letters (work, WAIT, idle, LIMT,
stop, done, off). The terminal is always restored on exit.

groups.title: Open Source templates
groups.body:
One-click installs for popular open-source apps. Each template declares its
official Docker image and required services (Postgres, Redis, etc.). Running
`ownstack oss install` creates a new OwnStack app on a provisioned stack,
links the required services, and deploys the image. Same catalog the
Extras → Open Source page in the web UI consumes.

What install does for you:
  - Creates the OwnStack app with the right needs_* flags so deploys
    install / link the right Dokku plugin services automatically.
  - Generates any required secrets (placeholders like SECRET_KEY,
    MEILI_MASTER_KEY) with SecureRandom.hex.
  - Mounts persistent volumes declared by the template (Ollama models,
    Qdrant storage, etc.) via `dokku storage:mount` before the deploy.
  - For templates that need a post-link env-var copy (currently Metabase:
    MB_DB_CONNECTION_URI from DATABASE_URL), a worker fires ~45 s after
    the initial deploy lands, sets the derived vars, and rebuilds.

Required secrets are auto-generated; you can read them after install
with `dokku config:show <app>` over SSH or via the app's config in
the web UI.

groups.title: Authentication
groups.body:
Sign in to the control plane. Tokens are stored in ~/.ownstack/config, or per
account under ~/.ownstack/profiles/<name> when using profiles.

With OWNSTACK_PROFILE=<name> set, login saves into that profile for this one
command (it does not change your default profile), so each account's token
stays in its own profile.

flags.desc: Direct token from Settings → API token.
With --token, save the token as profile NAME and switch the active profile to it. To add a profile WITHOUT switching, use `ownstack profile add`.

Label for the minted CLI token (defaults to this machine's hostname). Each name holds an independent token, so logging in on one machine never revokes another machine's token; re-login with the same name rotates only that token.

commands.name: profile
commands.summary: Manage multiple control-plane accounts (list, show, use, add).
commands.body:
Profiles let one machine hold tokens for several control-plane accounts.
Files live in ~/.ownstack/profiles/<name>. The active profile is recorded
in ~/.ownstack/config; any command can override it for a single invocation
with the OWNSTACK_PROFILE environment variable, which is the safest pattern
when multiple terminals or agents share the machine.

`profile add` creates a profile WITHOUT changing the active profile, so
concurrent work against other accounts is never disturbed. By contrast
`ownstack login --token TOKEN --profile NAME` creates the profile AND
switches the active profile to it.

be an account admin (for its own tenant) or a superuser (cross-tenant); the

workflows.title: First-time setup
steps: Install the CLI (curl install or local clone).
Run `ownstack login` and complete the browser flow.
Run `ownstack apps` to confirm you can see your account.

workflows.title: Generate and deploy a new app from scratch
steps: `cd myapp && ownstack git push --name=myapp --app=myapp` — push to ownstack Git and create the app.
`ownstack deploy --wait` — kick off the first deploy and stream the log.

workflows.title: Adopt an existing local repo into the control plane
steps: `ownstack remote -a my-app` — link the repo to an existing app.

workflows.title: Promote staging to production
steps: `ownstack pipeline add-staging` — creates the staging stage on the same stack and kicks off a staging deploy.
Test the staging deploy at its assigned domain (or pilot URL).
`ownstack pipeline promote` — re-deploys staging's last successful commit to the production stage.
`ownstack remote deploy-log` to tail the build.

workflows.title: Debug a failing deploy
steps: `ownstack remote deploy-log` — see the build/release log.
If the build failed, fix locally, commit, and `ownstack deploy --wait` again.
If the release (e.g. migrations) failed, fix in code and redeploy; for db connectivity see `ownstack ssh app <name>` or the Data → Health tab in the UI.

keys.desc: Seconds to wait on an ordinary control-plane request (default 15). Raise it when the control plane is slow; a timeout is reported as such rather than as an unreachable host. Long operations (deploys, restarts, stack reads over SSH) keep their own larger caps. Note OWNSTACK_CURL_OPTS cannot be used for this: it is passed before the built-in flags and curl honours the last one it sees.
